strengths: Strong empirical results: Best performance (SGM=0.311) across all 100 TALENT regression datasets, outperforming 31 methods including TabPFN-v2 and GBDTs
Comprehensive evaluation across three major benchmarks (TALENT: 300 datasets, TabArena-Lite: 51 datasets, meta-test: large scale) with thorough comparisons and multiple metrics

Excellent scalability properties: O(n log n) training and O(log n) inference complexity, enabling application to datasets with 500K samples; 2 orders of magnitude faster than alternatives on small datasets
Well-motivated technical approach combining tree-based partitioning with feature learning kernels; sensible modifications to kernel-RFM for tabular data structure
Native interpretability through AGOP analysis with concrete examples showing sensible feature importance; local feature learning capability addresses data heterogeneity
High reproducibility: Code released with scikit-learn API, detailed hyperparameter search spaces (Table A.1), and clear algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms A.1-A.5)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Leaf RFM is an incremental modification of existing kernel-RFM [29]; tree-based partitioning for kernels exists in TabPFN-v2; main contribution is combining existing techniques

Weaker classification performance: Ranks 3rd best on classification (after TabPFN-v2 and RealMLP) compared to 1st on regression; significantly limits practical applicability since classification is equally important

Scalability benefits delayed: Figure 5 shows super-linear scaling initially with log-linear benefits only at ~60K samples; for middle-range datasets (500-60K samples), advantage unclear and TabPFN-v2 sometimes faster

Critical ablations missing: No quantitative comparison of supervised vs unsupervised splitting; no ablation on leaf-RFM modifications; no sensitivity analysis on leaf size C (fixed at 60K); no comparison of full vs diagonal AGOP

Lack of theoretical justification: No theoretical guarantees on AGOP-based splitting quality; no analysis of when/why xRFM outperforms alternatives; gradient omission in AGOP computation (A.4) appears ad-hoc

Interpretability claims overstated: Section 5 examples cherry-picked from thousands of datasets; AGOP identifies directions but not causality; no systematic validation against ground-truth importance; limited comparison to Shapley values or other methods

Unclear hyperparameter sensitivity: Very large search spaces (Table A.1) with many tunable parameters; m (split model subsample size) not listed; no sensitivity analysis; validation split handling ('hold out training data') problematic for bias estimation
Incomplete comparisons: TabPFN-v2 couldn't run on all datasets; meta-test results from literature rather than direct reimplementation; different tuning intensities across methods

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 300+ datasets with rigorous benchmarking against 31 methods on three major benchmarks (TALENT, TabArena-Lite, meta-test)
Best performance on regression tasks across 100 datasets, with clear improvements in multiple aggregation metrics (SGMε, rank, Top-K metrics)
Strong scalability properties with O(n log n) training and O(log n) inference time, demonstrated on datasets up to 500K samples
Native interpretability through AGOP without stacking additional methods; Section 5 examples demonstrate sensible feature selections aligned with domain knowledge
Excellent inference speed achieving performance-efficiency Pareto frontier on TabArena-Lite
Well-written paper with detailed algorithmic descriptions, multiple large-scale experiments, and promised code availability
Practical solution to important problem: tabular data prediction, where progress has been limited despite commercial significance
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (kernel-RFM from [29], tree partitioning, AGOP) without fundamental innovation; the four leaf RFM modifications are straightforward adaptations

Uneven performance across problem types: convincing on regression but only 3rd ranked on classification tasks, substantially behind RealMLP on multi-class (>10 classes), undermining universal improvement claims
Insufficient justification for design choices: why only top eigenvector for splitting? Why median-based partitioning? Limited comparison to unsupervised splitting despite mentioning alternatives
No ablation studies on critical hyperparameters; leaf size C fixed at 60,000 without justification; large search spaces (Table A.1) with dataset-specific ranges raise reproducibility concerns

Interpretability validation is primarily anecdotal; lacks systematic validation against ground truth and no quantitative comparison to Shapley values or gradient-based importance (acknowledged as future work)
Incomplete experimental comparisons: TabPFN-v2 excluded from some benchmarks due to restrictions; meta-test uses literature results not head-to-head runs with identical hyperparameter tuning
Scaling advantage limited for practical datasets: Figure 5 shows super-linear scaling through ~60K samples; many real tabular datasets <50K where advantage is minimal
Missing failure case analysis and dataset-specific performance characterization; no systematic understanding of when method succeeds vs. alternative approaches
Statistical significance testing only applied to KRR/RFM comparisons, not main benchmark results; no confidence intervals on claimed improvements
Lack of theoretical analysis on when/why xRFM should outperform alternatives; no sample complexity bounds or formal justification of design choices

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 300+ datasets with rigorous benchmarking against 31+ methods across TALENT, TabArena-Lite, and meta-test benchmarks
Strong empirical performance on regression tasks (best on 100 TALENT regression datasets, good speed-accuracy tradeoff on large datasets up to 500K samples)
Clear practical contributions: addresses scalability of kernel methods, provides native interpretability via AGOP, promises code release with scikit-learn API
Technically sound algorithm design with well-motivated modifications to kernel-RFM (generalized Lp,q kernels, axis-aligned AGOP bias) and clear algorithmic descriptions
Concrete interpretability examples demonstrating sensible feature discovery and local feature learning benefits across real datasets (housing, tree species prediction, taxi tipping)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is a straightforward engineering combination of RFM (Radhakrishnan et al., 2024) with standard binary tree partitioning, lacking conceptual innovation expected at top-tier venues

Inconsistent empirical results: dominant on regression but only third-best on TALENT classification tasks; TabPFN-v2 often competitive or superior on TabArena-Lite classification benchmarks, limiting claimed broad applicability

Scalability claims need qualification: method exhibits super-linear scaling up to 60K samples (Fig. 5), with log-linear regime only emerging later; training times show only modest improvements over alternatives; O(log n) inference is standard for tree methods

Interpretability validation is weak: only 4 datasets shown with AGOP examples (risk of cherry-picking); no systematic comparison against SHAP, feature importance, or gradient-based methods; paper explicitly acknowledges missing this comparison; no user studies on actionability

Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: extensive tuning space (Table A.1) with unclear parameter importance; leaf size C=60,000 appears arbitrary without ablation; risk of overfitting to benchmarks; unequal tuning effort between xRFM and baselines (different search procedures across benchmarks)

Statistical rigor gaps: Wilcoxon tests provided only for limited comparisons (Fig. 4); many results lack error bars or confidence intervals; no analysis of practical vs. statistical significance of marginal differences

Local feature learning lacks systematic validation: Figure 2 is a toy example; Figure 7B shows marginal variation; no characterization of real datasets where local learning provides meaningful gains; unclear prevalence in practice

Technical clarity issues: split model trained only on m subsampled points with unclear representativeness; median-based splits don't guarantee balance with skewed projections; missing ablation on arbitrary design choices (e.g., why C=60,000?)

Presentation problems: Figure 3 difficult to parse with overlapping points; critical results relegated to appendices; narrative doesn't clearly articulate relative strengths/weaknesses across task types
